title: Acute pancreatitis: urgent assessment and recovery
intro: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas, an organ that helps digest food and produces hormones including insulin. It can become serious and needs urgent hospital assessment. Symptoms alone cannot confirm the diagnosis: other emergencies can also cause severe abdominal pain. This article explains what to discuss with the hospital team rather than how to treat a suspected attack at home.

sections.heading: Recognise symptoms that need urgent help
paragraphs: Severe upper abdominal pain, especially when it begins suddenly, persists or spreads to the back, needs urgent assessment. Vomiting, fever, a fast heartbeat or breathing difficulty can accompany it. Severe pain with breathlessness, fainting or a rapidly worsening condition requires emergency help. Do not drive yourself when seriously unwell. Tell the service about the symptoms and when they began rather than waiting until you are certain that the pancreas is the cause.

sections.heading: Understand how the diagnosis and cause are investigated
paragraphs: Blood tests, including pancreatic enzymes such as lipase, help assess the diagnosis. Ultrasound or other imaging may be used to look for gallstones or complications; not everyone needs every scan immediately. Gallstones and alcohol are common causes, but medicines, high blood fats and other conditions can contribute. Sometimes no cause is found initially. Give an accurate medicine and alcohol history without stopping prescribed medicines yourself.

sections.heading: Know what hospital care is trying to achieve
paragraphs: The team monitors circulation, breathing, kidney function and other signs of severity. Treatment may include intravenous fluids, pain relief and support with nausea and nutrition. Some people need intensive care. Antibiotics are used when an infection calls for them, not automatically for every inflamed pancreas. A blocked bile duct or another specific problem may require a procedure. Ask what each intervention is addressing and which changes would alter the plan.

sections.heading: Follow an individual plan for food and recovery
paragraphs: Do not impose fasting or a restrictive diet on yourself as a home treatment. The team decides when and how you can eat according to your condition and tolerance. If eating is not possible, specialist nutritional support may be needed. Recovery is variable, and feeling better does not remove every risk of complications. Before discharge, clarify what to eat, how to use prescribed medicines and whom to contact about new symptoms.

sections.heading: Address the cause and recognise setbacks
paragraphs: Follow-up may include discussing gallbladder surgery if gallstones caused the attack, reviewing medicines or managing blood fats. Ask about avoiding alcohol and support if alcohol dependence makes stopping difficult; withdrawal may need medical supervision. New or worsening pain, fever, repeated vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or jaundice after discharge needs prompt medical advice. Severe illness, collapse or breathing problems require emergency help. Do not assume every setback is normal healing.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: describing an urgent problem
examples.text: Someone develops strong upper abdominal pain spreading to the back and keeps vomiting. They seek urgent help, describe the symptoms and bring their medicine list if available. They do not delay care to search for a diet that might calm the pancreas.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: preparing for discharge
examples.text: A patient whose attack involved gallstones asks whether further treatment is needed to reduce recurrence, what follow-up is arranged and which symptoms mean returning urgently. They request written instructions, rather than assuming that leaving hospital means no further care is needed.

questions: What evidence supports the diagnosis and the suspected cause in my case?
What is the plan for pain relief, nutrition and monitoring for complications?
What follow-up addresses the cause, and which symptoms require urgent reassessment?
